nameStory: Field garlic gets its straightforward name from being the wild garlic species most commonly found growing in open fields and meadows. Unlike its woodland cousins, this member of the onion family prefers the sunny, well-drained spots that farmers and gardeners know well. The scientific name 'oleraceum' comes from Latin meaning 'vegetable' or 'herbal,' reflecting its edible nature.
description: Field garlic is a slender, wild member of the onion family that reaches about a foot tall. Like its garden relatives, it grows from an underground bulb and produces narrow, grass-like leaves that smell distinctly of garlic when crushed. The plant sends up a single flowering stem topped with a cluster of small flowers, though it's quite rare to spot in New England. This European native reproduces not just by seeds, but also by forming tiny bulblets right in the flower head.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves that smell strongly of garlic when crushed or bruised - the scent is unmistakable and much stronger than regular grass

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small flowers clustered at the top of a single stem, often mixed with tiny bulblets that look like miniature onions nestled among the blooms

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows about 12 inches tall in small clumps, with several narrow leaves emerging from the base and one central flowering stem

idTips.label: Bulb
idTips.description: Underground bulb that's small and white, similar to a tiny onion with papery outer layers that rustle when handled

habitat: Field garlic prefers dry, sunny locations with well-drained soil, living up to its name by growing in open fields, meadows, and disturbed areas. In New England, look for it along roadsides, in old pastures, and in other sunny spots where the soil isn't too wet. It thrives in areas that get full sun and doesn't compete well in shady or heavily wooded locations.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge from the ground, looking like thin grass but releasing that telltale garlic scent when touched.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs with small clusters of blooms and bulblets appearing at the stem tips, while leaves remain green and aromatic.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to yellow and die back as the plant prepares for winter dormancy, with seeds dispersing if flowers were successful.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to underground bulb, leaving no visible trace above ground until spring returns.

funFact: Field garlic is like a plant magician - it grows tiny baby bulbs right inside its flower clusters that drop to the ground and grow into new plants, essentially cloning itself in mid-air before your eyes!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with wild garlic (Allium vineale), but field garlic almost always has both flowers and bulblets mixed together in its flower head, while wild garlic often produces only bulblets with no flowers at all. Remember: field garlic is the 'mixed' species - it likes variety in its flower clusters.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'field garlic,' this plant is actually more closely related to onions than to true garlic, which can confuse gardeners familiar with cooking garlic. Like many members of the onion family, it's technically edible but should never be eaten unless you're absolutely certain of identification, as some grass-like plants can be toxic.
compareHints: Field garlic differs from wild garlic by having flower heads that contain both actual flowers and bulblets mixed together, while wild garlic usually produces only bulblets. It's much rarer than wild garlic in New England and tends to prefer drier, more open habitats than the woodland-loving wild leeks and ramps found in the region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wide leek stands out from other wild onions by having broad, flat leaves instead of narrow, tubular ones.
Wild garlic differs from other Alliums by its completely hollow, tubular leaves - wild leeks have flat, broad leaves, while chives have thin but solid leaves.
Unlike their larger cousins wild leek (ramps) which have broad, flat leaves, or wild garlic with its flat, grass-like foliage, chives have distinctively round, hollow leaves that are much thinner.

Among New England Alliums, garlic chives are unique for their flat, strap-like leaves - wild garlic has narrow tubular leaves, ramps have broad oval leaves, and regular chives have hollow cylindrical leaves.
Canadian Meadow Garlic differs from its cousin Wild Leek (ramps) by having thin, grass-like leaves rather than broad, flat leaves, and it grows in sunny areas rather than shaded forests.
Among New England's wild onions, nodding onion is the only one with distinctively drooping flower heads—wild garlic and field garlic hold their flowers upright in tight, rounded clusters.
Unlike other New England Alliums such as wild garlic, chives, or wild leeks that produce typical flower clusters, Egyptian Walking Onion is unmistakable with its bulblet clusters.
Among its Allium relatives, garlic is distinguished by its segmented bulb structure — wild onions and leeks have single, solid bulbs rather than the characteristic cloves.
Yellow onion stands out from other New England Alliums by its bright golden-yellow flowers - most wild onions and garlics have white, pink, or purple blooms.
Common onions differ from their wild Allium relatives by having distinctly hollow, tubular leaves and that familiar sharp kitchen-onion scent.
Ramsons stands out from other New England wild onions by having the broadest, flattest leaves in the genus - most other Alliums here have narrow, grass-like or tubular leaves.

Wild leek stands out from other New England Alliums by being much larger and more robust - while wild garlic and chives have thin, grass-like leaves, and ramps have broad leaves that disappear before flowering, wild leek maintains its broad, blue-green leaves right through the blooming period.
Unlike New England's native wild onions such as wild leek or wild garlic which have narrow, grass-like green leaves, Turkistan onion stands out with its broad, silvery-blue foliage.

Small Yellow Onion stands out dramatically from other New England Alliums due to its bright yellow flowers - most of our native and naturalized onions like Wild Garlic, Nodding Onion, and Wild Leek have white, pink, or purplish flowers.

Unlike other wild Alliums in New England like wild garlic or ramps, honey garlic has uniquely drooping, bell-shaped flowers rather than the upright, star-shaped or rounded flower clusters typical of most onion relatives.
